introduction-the-noisy-neighbor-problem.core: A SaaS tenant is a customer organisation. Sharing infrastructure between tenants is cheap, but one tenant's load spike, misconfiguration or breach can affect others: the noisy neighbour problem. Tenancy models range from fully pooled (shared everything) to fully siloed (dedicated stack per tenant), and the IaC structure you choose decides isolation, blast radius, cost and operational effort.

first_principles.problem: One enterprise customer's batch job saturates the shared database, slowing every other customer.
derivation: Map model to **IaC structure** and state.

analogy.title: Apartment building vs detached houses
analogy.story: Apartments share walls and plumbing (cheap, noisy); houses are isolated (expensive, quiet).
analogy.breaks: Buildings are fixed; tenants can be moved between models.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Isolation matched to price and compliance.

check.q: What is the noisy neighbour problem?
check.a: One tenant's heavy usage or failure degrades performance or availability for other tenants sharing the same resources.

strategy-1-module-per-tenant-the-pool-ap.core: The simplest IaC approach: one root module and one state, looping a tenant module with for_each over a map of tenants. Onboarding a tenant means adding a map entry. Everything is visible in one place, but every plan touches every tenant, a single bad change can affect all of them, state grows linearly, and plans slow down as tenants are added.

first_principles.problem: With 300 tenants in one state, a plan takes 25 minutes and a typo in the shared module breaks everyone.
truths: One state equals one blast radius.
derivation: Plan an **exit** to cells as tenants grow.

analogy.title: A single spreadsheet with a row per customer
analogy.story: Easy to see everything, but one bad formula breaks every row.
analogy.breaks: Spreadsheets recalc instantly; plans refresh every resource.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Add a line to onboard; but all tenants share one plan/apply.

check.q: What's the main risk of the pool approach as tenants grow?
check.a: Every change plans and applies against all tenants in one state, so mistakes affect everyone and plans become slow.

strategy-2-workspace-per-tenant-the-clon.core: Terraform workspaces give each tenant its own state from the same code: `terraform workspace select acme`, then apply with that tenant's tfvars. Blast radius shrinks to one tenant per apply, but all tenants must run identical code versions, upgrades mean looping applies over every workspace, workspace selection is implicit and error-prone, and visibility across tenants needs extra tooling.

first_principles.problem: Rolling a module upgrade to 200 tenant workspaces requires a fragile shell loop, and one run hits the wrong workspace.

analogy.title: Photocopies of one master document
analogy.story: Each customer gets a separate copy, but updating the master means re-copying for everyone, and it's easy to hand someone the wrong copy.
analogy.breaks: Photocopies are static; workspaces are live infrastructure.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Wrong workspace + tfvars combination fails at plan.

check.q: Why do workspaces force lockstep upgrades across tenants?
check.a: All workspaces share the same code directory, so you can't pin different module versions per tenant.

strategy-3-cell-based-directory-per-tena.core: Cell-based IaC generates a separate directory (its own root module and state) per tenant or per cell of tenants, each pinning its own module version. Tenants upgrade in waves (canary cells first), failures stay inside one cell, and the generated directories make each tenant's configuration explicit. Tooling (Terragrunt, scripts, Spacelift) creates cells from a template and orchestrates rollouts.

first_principles.problem: A bad upgrade must never take down all customers at once, and enterprise tenants need different upgrade timing.

analogy.title: Ships with watertight compartments
analogy.story: A breach floods one compartment, not the whole ship, and each can be repaired on its own schedule.
analogy.breaks: Compartments are identical; cells may run different versions temporarily.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: v4.2.0 proves itself in canary before wave 2.

code.text:
infrastructure/
  modules/tenant-stack/          # versioned
  cells/
    cell-001-canary/terragrunt.hcl   # ref=v4.2.0
    cell-002/terragrunt.hcl          # ref=v4.1.3
    enterprise-acme/terragrunt.hcl   # ref=v4.1.3, dedicated
  scripts/new-cell.sh

check.q: What key capability do cells add over workspaces?
check.a: Each cell pins its own module version, enabling staged (canary/wave) upgrades and per-tenant timing.
